title: GFW API client: geostore + tree cover loss
description:
## Files
- src/tools/gfw-api.ts (create)

## What to do
Create the core GFW API client module with these exported functions:

### 1. `createGeostore(lat: number, lng: number, radiusKm: number): Promise<GeostoreResult>`
- Build a bounding box polygon: `delta = radiusKm / 111.32`
- POST to `https://api.resourcewatch.org/v1/geostore` with body:
  ```json
  {"geojson":{"type":"FeatureCollection","features":[{"type":"Feature","properties":{},"geometry":{"type":"Polygon","coordinates":[[[lng-d,lat-d],[lng+d,lat-d],[lng+d,lat+d],[lng-d,lat+d],[lng-d,lat-d]]]}}]}}
  ```
- Return `{ hash: string, areaHa: number }`
- Use `User-Agent: Pi-Taina/1.0 (biodiversity-bot)` header
- No auth needed for this endpoint

### 2. `getTreeCoverLoss(apiKey: string, geostoreHash: string): Promise<TreeCoverResult>`
- GET `https://data-api.globalforestwatch.org/dataset/umd_tree_cover_loss/latest/query/json`
- Query params:
  - `sql`: `SELECT umd_tree_cover_loss__year, SUM(area__ha) as loss_ha FROM results WHERE umd_tree_cover_density_2000__threshold >= 30 GROUP BY umd_tree_cover_loss__year ORDER BY umd_tree_cover_loss__year`
  - `geostore_id`: the hash from createGeostore
  - `geostore_origin`: `rw`
- Header: `x-api-key: <apiKey>`
- IMPORTANT: Must follow redirects (the API returns 307 before 200)
- Return: `{ years: Array<{year: number, lossHa: number}>, totalLossHa: number, latestYear: number }`
- The `umd_tree_cover_loss__year` field is already the full year (2001, 2002, etc.)

### 3. `getTreeCoverExtent(geostoreHash: string): Promise<TreeExtentResult>`
- GET `https://api.resourcewatch.org/v1/umd-loss-gain`
- Query params: `geostore=<hash>&period=2001-01-01,2024-12-31&thresh=30`
- No auth needed
- Return: `{ areaHa: number, treeExtent2000Ha: number, treeExtent2010Ha: number, gainHa: number, lossHa: number }`

### Types to export
```typescript
interface GeostoreResult { hash: string; areaHa: number }
interface TreeCoverYear { year: number; lossHa: number }
interface TreeCoverResult { years: TreeCoverYear[]; totalLossHa: number; latestYear: number }
interface TreeExtentResult { areaHa: number; treeExtent2000Ha: number; treeExtent2010Ha: number; gainHa: number; lossHa: number }
interface GfwError { success: false; error: string }
```

All functions should catch network/HTTP errors and return `GfwError` on failure (use a union return type like the existing tools do).

Use native `fetch` — no new dependencies.

## Don't
- Don't import from env.ts — the apiKey is passed as a parameter
- Don't add any npm dependencies
- Don't implement fire or deforestation alert queries yet (separate task)
- Don't register any Pi agent tools (separate task)
acceptance_criteria: 1. src/tools/gfw-api.ts exists and exports createGeostore, getTreeCoverLoss, getTreeCoverExtent. 2. All types exported. 3. createGeostore builds correct bounding box polygon and calls RW API. 4. getTreeCoverLoss sends SQL query with x-api-key header and follows redirects. 5. getTreeCoverExtent calls RW API umd-loss-gain. 6. All functions return error objects on failure (never throw). 7. No new npm dependencies. 8. TypeScript compiles without errors.

## What to do
Create a skill file that instructs the Pi agent how to use the forest_report tool. Follow the exact same format as `skills/publish-observation/SKILL.md`.

### Content
```markdown
---
name: forest-monitoring
description: Query forest health data for any location using Global Forest Watch. Use when users ask about deforestation, fires, tree cover, or forest health near them or near their observations.
---

# Forest Monitoring

## When to Use
- User asks "how is the forest doing near me?" or similar
- User asks about deforestation, fires, tree cover loss
- After publishing an observation, to add forest context ("your toucan was spotted in an area that lost 35% of its forest")
- User shares a location and asks about environmental threats

## How to Use
1. You need GPS coordinates. If the user shared a Telegram location, use those. If they gave a place name, use geocode_location first.
2. Call forest_report with latitude, longitude, and optionally radiusKm (default 10km)
3. Present the results conversationally — do NOT dump raw numbers

## Presenting Results
- Lead with the most striking finding (e.g., "Your area has lost 35% of its forest since 2000")
- Use emoji sparingly: 🌳 for tree cover, 🔥 for fires, 🛰️ for deforestation alerts
- Round numbers for readability (314.67 ha → "about 315 hectares")
- Convert hectares to something relatable when useful ("that is about 440 football fields")
- If there are active fires or recent deforestation, highlight that urgently
- If the area is healthy (low loss, no alerts), celebrate it

## Attribution
Always include "Data: Global Forest Watch" at the end of forest reports.

## Don't
- Don't show raw JSON to users
- Don't present all data points — pick the 2-3 most meaningful
- Don't lecture about deforestation — let the numbers speak
- Don't call forest_report unless the user asked about forest/environment topics or you're adding context to an observation
```

- Don't add any code files — this is just the skill markdown

title: Generate tree cover loss chart image via QuickChart.io
description:
## Files
- src/tools/gfw-chart.ts (create)

## What to do
Create a module that generates a bar chart PNG image of tree cover loss by year using the QuickChart.io API (free, no auth, no dependencies — just a URL that returns a PNG).

### Function signature
```typescript
export async function generateTreeCoverLossChart(
  years: Array<{ year: number; lossHa: number }>,
  title?: string
): Promise<Buffer | null>
```

### How QuickChart.io works
You build a Chart.js config as JSON, URL-encode it, and fetch the PNG:
```
https://quickchart.io/chart?c={...chart config...}&w=600&h=400&bkg=white
```

### Chart config
Build a Chart.js v2 config object:
```javascript
{
  type: "bar",
  data: {
    labels: years.map(y => String(y.year)),  // Show last 10 years max
    datasets: [{
      label: "Tree Cover Loss (ha)",
      data: years.map(y => Math.round(y.lossHa)),
      backgroundColor: "rgba(228, 88, 62, 0.8)",  // GFW red-orange
      borderColor: "rgba(228, 88, 62, 1)",
      borderWidth: 1
    }]
  },
  options: {
    title: { display: true, text: title || "Tree Cover Loss", fontSize: 16 },
    legend: { display: false },
    scales: {
      yAxes: [{ ticks: { beginAtZero: true }, scaleLabel: { display: true, labelString: "Hectares" } }],
      xAxes: [{ scaleLabel: { display: true, labelString: "Year" } }]
    }
  }
}
```

### Implementation
1. Take the last 10 years of data (slice from end) to keep the chart readable
2. Build the Chart.js config object
3. JSON.stringify it, then URL-encode with encodeURIComponent
4. Fetch `https://quickchart.io/chart?c=${encoded}&w=600&h=400&bkg=white`
5. If response is OK, return the body as a Buffer
6. If fetch fails or returns non-200, return null (never throw)
7. Set a 10-second timeout on the fetch

### User-Agent
Use `User-Agent: Pi-Taina/1.0 (biodiversity-bot)` header.

## Don't
- Don't add any npm dependencies
- Don't use canvas or any server-side rendering
- Don't generate charts for fewer than 2 data points (return null)
- Don't include years with 0 loss in the chart (filter them out)

title: Epic: Pi-Tainá MVP — Telegram biodiversity bot on Pi agent
description:
## Goal
Build a self-hosted Telegram bot (Pi-Tainá) that replicates core Tainá functionality as a Pi agent. Each community deploys their own instance on a Mac Mini with their own Telegram bot token and ATProto community account.

## Architecture
- **Telegram**: grammY library for Telegram Bot API
- **Agent**: Pi coding agent SDK (`@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`) with `createAgentSession()`
- **ATProto**: Single community account using `@atproto/api` with app password auth (not OAuth)
- **Models**: API-based (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google keys via Pi's provider system)
- **Deployment**: Self-hosted on Mac Mini M4, easy setup

## Core Features (MVP)
1. Species identification from photos (vision AI)
2. Photo quality coaching (organism-specific tips)
3. Publish Darwin Core occurrence records to community ATProto PDS
4. Geocoding via Nominatim (+ Telegram location sharing)
5. General community assistant (collective intelligence)
6. Self-extending: communities can ask Tainá to build new skills

## Key Design Decisions
- One ATProto account per community (not per user)
- Telegram user info (ID, username, display name) stored in Darwin Core `recordedBy` field
- Per-user sessions within the community
- Groups: responds only when @mentioned or when photos are sent
- DMs: always responds
- Community personality customizable via AGENTS.md / skills
- All Tainás share core primitives, each community customizes personality/language/local knowledge

## Success Criteria
- Bot responds to DMs and group @mentions
- Photos auto-trigger species identification + coaching
- Users can publish observations to ATProto PDS via inline keyboards
- Telegram location sharing works for coordinates
- Easy setup: clone repo, set env vars, run one command

## What to do
Create a comprehensive README for Pi-Tainá that explains what it is, how to set it up, and how to deploy it on a Mac Mini.

**Sections:**

1. **Header**: Pi-Tainá logo area (just text for now), one-line description: "A self-hosted Telegram bot for community biodiversity documentation, powered by Pi agent"

2. **What is Pi-Tainá?**: 
   - Community biodiversity AI assistant on Telegram
   - Identifies species from photos, coaches on photo quality, publishes Darwin Core occurrence records
   - Each community runs their own instance with their own personality
   - Built on Pi coding agent — communities can ask Tainá to build new capabilities
   - Part of the GainForest network

3. **Quick Start** (numbered steps):
   - Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, npm
   - Clone the repo
   - `npm install`
   - Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in values
   - `npm start`

4. **Configuration** (env vars table):
   | Variable | Required | Description |
   | TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN | Yes | From @BotFather on Telegram |
   | ANTHROPIC_API_KEY | Yes | Anthropic API key for Claude |
   | ATPROTO_HANDLE | No* | Community ATProto/Bluesky handle |
   | ATPROTO_PASSWORD | No* | App password for the ATProto account |
   | PI_MODEL | No | Override default model (default: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514) |
   | SPECIES_ID_MODEL | No | Model for species identification (default: claude-sonnet-4-20250514) |
   
   *Required for publishing observations

5. **Setting up Telegram Bot**: 
   - Message @BotFather on Telegram
   - /newbot, choose name and username
   - Copy the token
   - Optional: set bot description and profile photo

6. **Setting up ATProto Account**:
   - Create a Bluesky account for your community (e.g., taina-amazon.bsky.social)
   - Go to Settings → App Passwords → Create app password
   - Use the handle and app password in .env

7. **Customizing for Your Community**:
   - Edit AGENTS.md to customize personality, language, local knowledge
   - Add skills in ./skills/ directory
   - Tainá can also build skills herself when asked

8. **How It Works** (brief architecture):
   - Telegram message → Pi agent → AI response
   - Photos auto-trigger species identification
   - Observations published to ATProto PDS as Darwin Core records

9. **Running as a Service** (Mac Mini deployment):

```markdown
name: species-identification
description: Identify species from photos and coach users on photo quality. Use when a user sends a photo of a plant, animal, fungus, or other organism. Handles the full observation flow: identification, quality coaching, and multi-photo accumulation.
---

# Species Identification

## Photo Observation Flow
When a user sends a photo:
1. ALWAYS call identify_species to analyze it
2. Share the identification results: common name, scientific name, conservation status
3. Review the imageQuality assessment and coach on photo quality:
   - If quality is "excellent"/"good": compliment and offer to publish
   - If quality is "fair": share ID first, then gently suggest improvements with organism-specific tips
   - If quality is "poor": still share ID, give 1-2 actionable tips, offer to publish anyway
4. Ask if they want to publish as a permanent observation record
5. NEVER refuse to publish — you are a coach, not a gatekeeper

## Photo Quality Coaching Tips
Use these organism-specific tips after identification:
- Plants: photograph leaves (shape + veins), flowers/fruit, bark, whole plant habit
- Birds: face and beak (most important), plumage pattern, overall shape. Walk normally near birds, don't sneak.
- Insects: dorsal view from above, wing pattern, close-up essential
- Fungi: cap from above, underside showing gills/pores (CRITICAL), stem, substrate
- Reptiles/Amphibians: head shape, body pattern, scale/skin texture
- Marine/Shells: shell opening/aperture, overall shape, something for scale
- General: if too far away, suggest cropping the photo on their phone

## Multi-Photo Observation Flow
When coaching on photo quality, actively encourage multiple angles:
- After first photo: identify the species, then suggest 1-2 specific additional angles based on the organism group
- After each additional photo: acknowledge it, note what it adds, suggest more if key features are still missing
- When you have enough good photos (or the user says they are done): offer to publish
- When publishing: ALL accumulated photos are attached to the observation record
- After publishing: photos are cleared for the next observation

Example flow:
- User sends photo of a mushroom from above
- Tainá: "This looks like Amanita muscaria! 🍄 Great top-down shot. Could you also photograph the underside showing the gills? That is the most important feature for confirming mushroom IDs."
- User sends photo of gills
- Tainá: "Perfect, I can see the white free gills clearly! One more — the stem base would help rule out look-alikes. Or we can publish with these 2 photos if you prefer."
- User: "publish it"
- Tainá publishes with both photos attached

Key principles:
- Never demand more photos — always offer to publish with what you have
- Be specific about WHAT to photograph and WHY (not just "take more photos")
- Celebrate each additional photo the user sends
- 2-3 good photos from different angles is ideal, but 1 is fine too
```

```markdown
name: publish-observation
description: Publish biodiversity occurrence records to the community ATProto PDS. Use after species identification when the user wants to record their observation. Handles location collection, Darwin Core record creation, and citizen science education.
---

# Publish Observation

## Publishing Flow
When publishing an occurrence record:
1. Ensure you have: species ID, photo, and location
2. If location is missing, ask the user to share their Telegram location (tap the 📎 attachment button → Location)
3. If they give a text location instead, use geocode_location to get coordinates
4. Call publish_occurrence with all available data
5. Celebrate the publication! "You just contributed to biodiversity data! 🌿"

## Location Handling
- If the user sends a Telegram location message, use those exact GPS coordinates
- If the user types a place name, use geocode_location to convert to coordinates
- Always prefer GPS coordinates over text locations for accuracy
- Never refuse to publish just because location is missing — ask once, then respect their choice

## Citizen Science Education
Weave these in naturally — one sentence at a time, never lecture:
- "Your observations help scientists track species populations over time"
- "Location data helps map species ranges and detect climate change impacts"
- On first publication: "You just contributed to global biodiversity data! Every observation counts. 🎉"
- After multiple publications: "You're building a great record of your local biodiversity!"
```

```markdown
name: geocoding
description: Convert text location descriptions to GPS coordinates using the geocode_location tool. Use when a user provides a place name instead of sharing their Telegram GPS location.

# Geocoding

## When to Use
- User says "I saw it near the river in Manaus" → geocode "river, Manaus, Brazil"
- User says "Central Park" → geocode "Central Park, New York"
- User provides a locality name during the publishing flow

## How to Use
1. Call geocode_location with the place description as query
2. Optionally pass a countryCode (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2) to narrow results
3. The tool returns: latitude, longitude, formatted address, locality, country, stateProvince
4. Use the returned coordinates for publish_occurrence

## Tips
- Be specific in queries: "Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil" works better than just "Manaus"
- If the first result seems wrong, ask the user to clarify
- Always prefer Telegram GPS location sharing over geocoding for accuracy
```

- Do NOT add frontmatter fields beyond name and description
- Do NOT create nested subdirectories inside skill folders (keep flat: SKILL.md only for now)

## What to do
Create the Pi agent integration layer. This manages per-user agent sessions and registers Tainá's custom tools with the Pi SDK.

**Export:**

```typescript
import type { IncomingMessage } from "./telegram.ts";

// Get or create a Pi agent session for a Telegram user
// Sessions are keyed by Telegram user ID
// Each session persists to disk under ./data/sessions/{userId}/
export async function getOrCreateSession(userId: number): Promise<AgentSession>

// Send a message to the agent and collect the full response
// Handles: text messages, photo context, location context
// Returns the agent's text response
export async function sendToAgent(
  msg: IncomingMessage
): Promise<string>

// Cleanup / dispose all sessions
export async function disposeAllSessions(): Promise<void>
```

**Behavior:**

1. **Session management**:
   - Maintain a `Map<number, AgentSession>` keyed by Telegram user ID
   - On first message from a user, create a new session via `createAgentSession()`
   - Use `SessionManager.create("./data/sessions/{userId}")` for persistent sessions
   - Configure `AuthStorage.create()` and `ModelRegistry` once at module level

2. **Agent configuration**:
   - Default model: read from env `PI_MODEL` with fallback to `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514"`
   - Set API key via `authStorage.setRuntimeApiKey("anthropic", process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)`
   - Also set OpenAI and Google keys if present in env
   - Load AGENTS.md from project root (Pi does this automatically via DefaultResourceLoader)
   - Load skills from `./skills/` directory (Pi does this automatically)

3. **Custom tools registration**:
   Register 3 custom tools via the `customTools` option in `createAgentSession()`:

   **a) `identify_species`**:
   - Description: "Identify a species from a photo that the user sent. Call this when the user sends a photo of a plant, animal, fungus, or other organism."
   - Input schema: `{ userContext?: string }` (the photo data comes from session state, not tool input)
   - Implementation: reads the latest photo from a per-session state store, calls `identifySpecies()` from tools/identify-species.ts, returns the JSON result as a string
   
   **b) `publish_occurrence`**:
   - Description: "Publish a biodiversity occurrence record to the community ATProto PDS. Use after identifying a species when the user confirms they want to publish."
   - Input schema: `{ scientificName: string, vernacularName?: string, decimalLatitude?: number, decimalLongitude?: number, locality?: string, country?: string, countryCode?: string, habitat?: string, behavior?: string, individualCount?: number, occurrenceRemarks?: string, eventDate?: string }`
   - Implementation: calls `publishOccurrence()` from tools/publish-occurrence.ts, passing the tool input + current photo data + current Telegram user from session state
   
   **c) `geocode_location`**:
   - Description: "Convert a text location description to GPS coordinates. Use when the user provides a place name instead of GPS coordinates."
   - Input schema: `{ query: string, countryCode?: string }`
   - Implementation: calls `geocodeLocation()` from tools/geocode-location.ts, returns the result as JSON string

4. **Message construction for sendToAgent()**:
   - If msg has photo: store photo data in per-session state, then prompt with: "The user sent a photo. [Photo is available for analysis]. {msg.text || ""}"
   - If msg has location: prompt with: "The user shared their GPS location: latitude {lat}, longitude {lon}. {msg.text || ""}"
   - If msg has only text: prompt with the text directly
   - The prompt should include user context: "Message from {user.displayName} (Telegram user ID: {user.id})"

5. **Response collection**:
   - Subscribe to session events
   - Collect all `text_delta` events from `message_update` into a string
   - Wait for `agent_end` event
   - Return the collected text

- Do NOT handle Telegram-specific sending/receiving — that is in telegram.ts
- Do NOT add inline keyboard logic
- Do NOT add the system prompt here — that goes in AGENTS.md (next task)
- Do NOT block on tool execution UI — tools run automatically (no permission gates)

```markdown
- Celebrate their efforts to protect nature and document biodiversity
- Respectful of indigenous and local knowledge — never dismiss traditional names or practices

- Biodiversity documentation and monitoring

## Photo Observation Flow
When a user sends a photo:
1. ALWAYS call identify_species to analyze it
2. Share the identification results: common name, scientific name, conservation status
3. Review the imageQuality assessment and coach on photo quality:
   - If quality is "excellent"/"good": compliment and offer to publish
   - If quality is "fair": share ID first, then gently suggest improvements with organism-specific tips
   - If quality is "poor": still share ID, give 1-2 actionable tips, offer to publish anyway
4. Ask if they want to publish as a permanent observation record
5. NEVER refuse to publish — you are a coach, not a gatekeeper

## Photo Quality Coaching Tips (use after identification)

- Birds: face and beak (most important), plumage pattern, overall shape. Walk normally near birds, don't sneak.
- Insects: dorsal view from above, wing pattern, close-up essential
- Fungi: cap from above, underside showing gills/pores (CRITICAL), stem, substrate

2. If location is missing, ask the user to share their Telegram location (tap the 📎 attachment button → Location)
```

title: Add reverseGeocodeAdmin function to gfw-api.ts
description:
## Files
- src/tools/gfw-api.ts (modify)

## What to do
Add a new exported function that reverse-geocodes a GPS point to its GADM administrative boundaries.

### Function signature
```typescript
export async function reverseGeocodeAdmin(
  apiKey: string,
  lat: number,
  lng: number
): Promise<AdminBoundaryResult | GfwError>
```

### How it works
GET `https://data-api.globalforestwatch.org/dataset/gadm_administrative_boundaries/latest/features?lat={lat}&lng={lng}&z=10`
- Header: `x-api-key: <apiKey>`
- Must follow redirects (`redirect: "follow"`)

The response returns an array of features at different admin levels. Parse them into:

```typescript
export interface AdminBoundary {
  level: number;           // 0=country, 1=state, 2=municipality
  name: string;            // "Altamira", "Pará", "Brazil"
  type: string;            // "Municipality", "State", "Country"
  geostoreId: string;      // gfw_geostore_id — ready for queries
  areaHa: number;          // gfw_area__ha
  country: string;         // always present
  state?: string;          // name_1 (for level 1 and 2)
  municipality?: string;   // name_2 (for level 2 only)
  isoCode: string;         // gid_0 e.g. "BRA", "MEX"
}

export interface AdminBoundaryResult {
  success: true;
  boundaries: AdminBoundary[];  // sorted by level ascending (0, 1, 2)
  municipality?: AdminBoundary; // convenience: the adm2 boundary if found
  state?: AdminBoundary;        // convenience: the adm1 boundary if found
  country?: AdminBoundary;      // convenience: the adm0 boundary if found
}
```

### Parsing the response
The API returns `{ data: Array<{...}> }`. Each item has:
- `adm_level`: "0", "1", or "2" (string!)
- `country`: country name
- `name_1`: state/province name (level 1+)
- `name_2`: municipality/district name (level 2)
- `engtype_2`: "Municipality", "District", etc. (level 2)
- `gfw_geostore_id`: UUID string — this is the key output
- `gfw_area__ha`: area in hectares
- `gid_0`: ISO country code ("BRA", "MEX")

For each item, build an `AdminBoundary`:
- `level`: parseInt(adm_level)
- `name`: name_2 || name_1 || country (most specific available)
- `type`: engtype_2 || "State" (for level 1) || "Country" (for level 0)
- `geostoreId`: gfw_geostore_id
- `areaHa`: gfw_area__ha
- `country`: country
- `state`: name_1 (if present)
- `municipality`: name_2 (if present)
- `isoCode`: gid_0

Sort boundaries by level ascending. Set convenience fields (municipality, state, country) from the parsed array.

### Edge cases
- Ocean points or points outside GADM coverage: return empty boundaries array (success: true, boundaries: [])
- Missing gfw_geostore_id on a boundary: skip that boundary (don't include it)

## Don't
- Don't modify any existing functions
- Don't add npm dependencies
- Don't remove the existing createGeostore function (it's still useful as fallback)
